title: Turn budget, not capability, gates the DCU task set: 21 tasks qualify at two turns, 25 at four and 27 at six, and the two that never do fail for reasons no budget reaches

observation:
Half the failures were budget. Four tasks that had reached their token limit with nothing qualified reached a confirmed endpoint when given four turns instead of two, with no other change -- same model, same shapes, same commit. That includes attention_decode, which had faulted three times before, and layernorm_gamma_beta_backward and per_channel_moments, each of which had failed twice.

The mechanism is visible in the event counts rather than inferred: a refusal arrives after the author has written the thing, so recovering from one costs a turn, and a task whose first attempt draws a verifier refusal has one turn left at the two-turn budget. softsign's successful run reaches event 41 against roughly 28 for a two-turn run of the same task.

The four that did not convert fail for reasons more turns did not reach. softmax drew a different frontend refusal on each of three runs -- an unsupported `range`, then an undeclared name, then `broadcast takes one value and an explicit axis` together with an alias assignment -- which reads as the authoring surface rather than any one gap. gemm_silu and gemm_bias both evaluated candidates and qualified none, so those reached the device and lost on their measurement.

Worth recording and not worth explaining yet: none of the eight larger-budget runs drew a provider fault, and channel_absmax_scale is among them -- the task that had invoked Bash on four of four attempts at the smaller budget (F-2026-09-17-010). Eight runs is not enough to say the budget changed that, and the two differ in more than budget, since a longer run also spends more of its turns past the point where the task statement is fresh. It is a coincidence worth a second look, not a result.

Extended to six turns, and the curve closes. Twenty-one tasks qualified at two turns, twenty-five at four, twenty-seven at six, out of twenty-nine. Both of the six-turn converts had failed twice before: softmax, and channel_absmax_scale, which is also the task that had invoked Bash on four of four attempts at two turns and adhered at both larger budgets.

softmax is the clearest case of what the turns buy. Its five refusals across four runs are five different ones, never repeating -- an unsupported `range`, an undeclared name, a leading literal where the order carries meaning, a malformed broadcast, an alias assignment. It was tempting to read that as the authoring surface being the binding constraint in a way budget could not fix. It is not: each distinct refusal costs one turn to recover from, and a task that trips several needs enough turns to absorb them. Given six it qualifies.

The two that never qualify fail for reasons outside this axis, and the distinction matters for how a sweep is read. gemm_bias cannot qualify on any target at any budget -- it was run at two and four turns and not at six, because the reason is a tolerance and not a budget, because no fp32 accumulation order meets its mixed_magnitude tolerance (F-2026-09-18-004). An earlier version of this sentence said that tolerance admitted only sequential accumulation, which is what that record went on to retract; the conclusion here was unaffected but the reason cited was dead for a while, and a record is not corrected by correcting the one it points at. gemm_silu's baseline passes every validation case and its candidate fails all five by 0.5 to 100.8 -- a wrong kernel, caught by the oracle, which is the harness working rather than failing. So of twenty-eight tasks that can qualify, twenty-seven do.
proposed_change:
No Compiler or Lab change. What this establishes is about how a DCU sweep should be run rather than about the harness: two turns is below the point where a task can recover from its first verifier refusal, and a sweep at that budget measures the authoring surface's first-attempt hit rate rather than what the loop can reach.

If a sweep's purpose is coverage, six turns is the setting that reaches it: four leaves two tasks short that six converts, and the per-task cost is repaid by not re-running them. A task that qualifies once is worth more than two that do not. If its purpose is to find authoring-surface defects, two turns surfaces them faster and this record is an argument for reading those sweeps as diagnostics rather than as results.

The provider-fault observation should be checked against a matched pair before anyone acts on it -- the same tasks at both budgets, counted -- rather than folded into F-2026-09-17-010 as though it were established.
